children: By Barbara Kollmeyer
Ulf Lindahl worries a Korea-like crash is coming for the S&P 500
Market veteran Ulf Lindahl is just as convinced that a 40% stock market crash is coming as he was before the October 1987 meltdown, as his proprietary momentum model had been raising the alarm.

"We happened to have a conference a few days before [the crash], and we'd already told them that we have a sell signal, and 'If you want to go out and sell now, you shoud do that,'"  Lindahl, the chief executive officer and founder of research and advisory firm Currency Research Associates, told MarketWatch in an interview on Thursday.  He said none of those attendees did and "the next morning they woke up to the crash."

"Right after the crash, we told people to buy stocks back because we saw a secular trend," he said. The strategists would be proved right  as Wall Street stocks would go onto recover, with the 1990s bull market to follow. These days, though, he sees as a historically overvalued stock market and average profit margins at a record near 12%, versus the 6% average.

He fears investors will suffer a repeat of what happened earlier this year, when roughly 40% was wiped off Korean stocks KR:180721 over a few weeks. While the Kospi  - seen as a leading indicator for AI investments - has struggled to recover from the summer rout, the index remains up 25% for 2026.

"Our view is that once the market falls, it falls so fast that it doesn't matter if it was up 5% or 10% this year-they've missed that entire gain, it would just be wiped out immediately, just like in Korea," said Lindahl. "Retail investors should just get out of stocks-because they're going to crash, and you can always buy them back later."

A second reason behind a looming selloff is what his long-term momentum model, which measures how far an asset is from the moving average, is saying. "It's way overbought and has turned down, and that to us always tells us that the steam has run out."
Ulf Lindahl, CEO, Currency Research Associates
Lindahl developed his model while at A.G. Bisset Associates, the now-closed currency management specialist he co-founded and ran, also serving as chief investment officer, for nearly 40 years.

He pairs the model with 150 charts across currencies, bonds and global equities, with cycles, secular trends, and fundamentals also weighed up.  The result helps confirm when a trend is about to change and reverse, but has led to some contrarian stances, because "when prices get overbought, everybody's bullish and happy, and we're saying 'Hey, wait, it's time to cool it.'"

Apart from the 1987 crash, his model successfully nailed the bottom for oil in 2016, its peak in 2022, and the bottom last year. However, it wrongly forecast a dollar decline in 2016, instead of the decade-long sideways move. Lindahl maintains the dollar has been supported by foreign buyers of U.S. tech stocks and central banks buying stocks instead of bonds, but expects those flows will reverse.

He's been urging clients since last year to prepare for a bear market in stocks in his "Review of Emerging Trends" advisory report that he started in 1984. The S&P 500 SPX is in the fourth year of a bull market, and holding onto a 10% gain this year. Over three years, the index has returned 71%, and 61% over five years, making it a tough market for investors to turn their backs on.
For the institutions that don't want to try timing the market, Lindhal advises switching to a 40/60 portfolio, meaning more bonds than stocks.

The equity portion should focus partly on non-U.S. stocks, as their related currencies will rise and that will buffer any losses from a weak dollar. Investors who must have stocks should hold energy as well as gold- and silver-mining companies, he said.
Opinion: Gold and silver are supposed to protect against inflation. So why are both metals tumbling instead?

His advice is that investors put money in Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA stocks, because it holds older, steady companies not as overvalued as AI stocks, and when the dot-com bubble burst, declines were led by the Nasdaq Composite COMP and S&P 500 SPX, in that order.

For institutions who want to time the market, he's advises clearing out of stocks and doubling down on bonds, specifically short-term maturities, and then after the market crashes, buy stocks and ride the next bull market higher. He also recommends food exposure through corn  (C00) and wheat (W00), due to ongoing wars and droughts caused by El Niño that he sees causing a wheat shortage next year.

Another big prediction from Lindahl is West Texas Intermediate crude (CL.1) hitting $500 per barrel by 2030, a view his firm has held for several years. The path to that is $147 per barrel by next February and $330 per barrel by April 2028.

Wall Street, to put it mildly, does not concur. Goldman Sachs for instance is predicting U.S. crude prices will average $78 a barrel in 2027, and drop to $70 by the end of next year, driven by stronger supply and weaker demand, notably from China.
History shows oil has seen massive surges before.

"Most people think we're completely nuts, but that has happened twice over two decades in the past," he said, of such a steep climb. In both the 1970-1980 and 1998-2008 periods, oil prices surged over 1,100% and "the world economy did not collapse and oil consumption continued to grow relentlessly," he said.

"But we did have severe recessions in 1980 and 2008 but not just because oil prices had surged +1,150% in the decade leading up to those years," he said, adding that few saw gold surging from $2,000 an ounce to $5,000, though that also happened recently.

"The main argument is that global oil production is peaking and that oil production cannot be increased due to geological factors and the U.S. shale's peaking while the demand for oil continues to grow. It opens a gap that can only be closed by higher prices and consumers shifting away from oil, but this will take time, and in the next four years prices will therefore surge," said Lindahl.

Advising clients to buy oil since October 2025, he pointed to a "largely ignored" report last year from the International Energy Agency that found 80% of the 15,000 global oil and gas wells it looked at were in decline. He is of the view that shale-oil production in the U.S. is peaking.

"Once the U.S. shale starts to drop, then there's not enough oil in the rest of the world that can replace that. And as a result, the global oil production will peak, and that would be as consequential, if not more, than in 1970 when our conventional oil peaked."

He also pointed to the historical correlation between oil and gold prices. "Whenever they get out of line, which has happened nine times since 1970, the oil prices rises on average more than 60% in the first six months after the ratio peaks," he said, adding that that ratio peaked earlier this year and oil climbed more than 60% over the next six months or so.

"Oil is also still 'dirt cheap' when adjusted for inflation since the 1970s and as well for the cumulative inflation of 30% in the past six years. Three-dollar gas is now $4 gas due to inflation and $100 oil is equal to $130 oil," Lindahl said.
-Barbara Kollmeyer
